title: Seeing Like a School: Categories, Maps, Streets and Winks
author: David Didau
summary: Drawing on institutional sociology and cognitive science, this essay examines how schools necessarily simplify complex daily reality to make institutions manageable. Yet these simplifications—categories like 'low ability' or labels for struggling teachers—can harden into self-fulfilling prophecies. Institutions don't merely use categories; they think with them, shaping what gets noticed and what gets ignored. The author synthesizes work by anthropologist Mary Douglas on institutional memory, psychologist Albert Michotte on causal inference, and political scientist James C. Scott on administrative legibility to argue that schools often mistake the proxies they create (grades, percentages, behavior codes) for the reality those proxies represent. Educators need methods for thinking beyond institutionalized categories to see both the mechanisms that drive problems and the possibilities for change.
points: School categorization systems (timetables, labels, data systems) are practical necessities but risk becoming institutions' primary way of thinking, obscuring rather than revealing reality.
The halo effect and fundamental attribution error combine to make schools overestimate individual disposition and underestimate context when interpreting student struggles.
Once a category becomes embedded in registers, seating plans, and meeting agendas, it steers institutional attention in ways that feel natural rather than like active human decisions.
Numerical proxies and standardized measures improve administrative legibility but destroy the local knowledge that made original arrangements work.
Leadership requires recognizing when institutional categories have become obstacles to precise problem diagnosis and more effective intervention.
quotes: Institutions direct individual memory and channel our perceptions into forms compatible with the relations they authorize. Once a category becomes institutionally useful, evidence is interpreted in ways that reinforce it.

A label such as 'low ability' may begin as a rough description of prior attainment, but it can soon affect the work a child is given, the questions they are asked and the explanations we reach for when progress stalls.
What begins as institutional shorthand becomes an explanation, and eventually a self-fulfilling prophecy. This is one of the most dangerous features of institutional life.

Schools have their own predictable ways to make it simpler for those in charge to pull levers in the hope of making meaningful change. The danger comes when we treat proxies as the things they are meant to represent.
Rather than asking, 'How do we fix this faulty individual?', the better, though more awkward, question is, 'What conditions are making these responses more likely?'

Leaders cannot run a school without shared names for recurring problems. But stability has a price: once a category becomes institutionally useful, evidence is interpreted in ways that reinforce it.” Archived from David Didau on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
